```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 8, fig.height = 4.5)
has_plots <- requireNamespace("ggplot2", quietly = TRUE) &&
  requireNamespace("patchwork", quietly = TRUE) &&
  requireNamespace("viridisLite", quietly = TRUE)
```

This vignette goes through the classic analysis of an aquatic mesocosm
experiment with a chemical: the effects on each population, summarised as
no observed effect concentrations (NOEC) with their minimum detectable
differences (MDD), and the effects on the community, with principal response
curves (PRC). It points out every decision that changes the results and the
argument that controls it.

```{r}
library(cosmet)
```

## The data

`azoxy` holds the counts of the experiment of Amador et al. (2024): 24
outdoor mesocosms with the communities of two habitats of the Albufera
Natural Park, a eutrophic lake and a water spring, exposed to the fungicide
azoxystrobin (controls and 2, 20 and 200 µg/L, applied on days 0 and 14,
three mesocosms each), sampled 7 days before the first application and 7,
21, 35 and 56 days after it. Each habitat is a separate experiment; here we
use the macroinvertebrates of the eutrophic lake, counted as the individuals
caught in two traps per mesocosm and date.

```{r}
macro <- subset(azoxy, community == "macroinvertebrates" & habitat == "eutrophic_lake")
head(macro[macro$abundance > 0, ])
```

## A validated experiment

`meso_data()` takes one row per mesocosm, time and taxon. The treatment here
is the concentration itself; the control is the level `"0"`.

```{r}
d <- meso_data(
  macro,
  mesocosm_col = "tank", time_col = "day", treatment_col = "concentration",
  concentration_col = "concentration", taxon_col = "taxon", value_col = "abundance",
  control = "0", zero_fill = FALSE, unit = "individuals/sample",
  concentration_unit = "µg/L", applications = c(0, 14)
)
d
check_design(d)
```

`zero_fill` has no default because it is a decision about the data. These
tables already have a zero for every taxon looked for and not found, so
nothing needs filling. Tables that store only the taxa found need
`zero_fill = TRUE`, and, if some sample had no taxa at all, the list of
analysed samples in `samples`; a mesocosm that was not sampled is never
filled with zeros. Recorded `NA` values stay unknown.

## Which taxa can be evaluated

`taxon_eligibility()` summarises each taxon in the controls only, so that a
taxon is not discarded because it declined in the treatments.

```{r}
elig <- taxon_eligibility(d, min_control_mean = 3)
elig[order(-elig$control_mean), c("taxon", "control_mean", "control_frequency", "eligible")][1:8, ]
```

The tests below use all taxa; `taxa = elig$taxon[elig$eligible]` would
restrict them.

## The scale of the analyses

Counts are analysed as $\ln(A x + 1)$. Amador et al. (2024) used
$A = 2$ for macroinvertebrates (33.3 for phytoplankton and 10 for
zooplankton, also in `s11_thresholds`). The original counts stay in `value`.

```{r}
d <- transform_response(d, A = 2)
```

## Population effects: Williams' test

`test_control()` compares every concentration with the control for each
taxon and date. Williams' test assumes a monotonic response and starts at
the highest concentration, stopping at the first non-significant one. Both
directions are tested (`direction = "both"`, p-values doubled), at
`alpha = 0.05`.

```{r}
tw <- test_control(d, method = "williams")
tw
```

Two options of the step-down procedure give different NOECs. With
`step_variance = "all"` (default) every step uses the variance and the
isotonic means of all groups, as Williams (1971, 1972); with `"reduced"`,
each step re-analyses the control and the doses up to the one tested, as
the original analysis script of the authors. The null distribution of the
statistic is simulated (`n_sim` draws) with a fixed seed, so results are
reproducible; the global random number stream is not changed.

## NOECs and consistent effects

`derive_noec()` turns the tests into NOECs and LOECs. With
`s11_criteria()` it also applies the four criteria of Text S11 of Amador et
al. (2024) for a consistent, treatment-related effect: (a) a significant
effect in a single direction; (b) enough abundance, here at least 3
individuals per sample in the control mean for decreases; (c) means on the
original scale that follow the direction of the effect; (d) no effect in
the same direction before the application (`pre_times`).

```{r}
noec <- derive_noec(tw, pre_times = -7, criteria = s11_criteria("macroinvertebrates"))
noec
```

The full table keeps every taxon and date with its status and criteria, so
that every exclusion can be checked:

```{r}
res <- as.data.frame(noec)
res[res$crit_a %in% TRUE, c("taxon", "time", "direction", "noec_label", "crit_b", "crit_c",
                            "crit_d", "selected")]
```

`noec_table()` lays the NOECs out for a report (arrows mark the direction):

```{r}
noec_table(noec, selected = TRUE)
```

The thresholds of criterion b carry their units: those of phytoplankton are
in cells/mL and are converted if the data are in cells/L; incompatible units
are an error.

```{r, eval = has_plots, fig.height = 6}
plot_noec(noec, xlab = "Day")
```

Dunnett's test does not assume a monotonic response; a significant
concentration with a non-significant one above it is flagged in the column
`consistent`:

```{r}
td <- test_control(d, method = "dunnett")
nd <- derive_noec(td, pre_times = -7)
noec_table(nd, selected = TRUE)
```

## Minimum detectable differences

A non-significant result is not proof that there is no effect.
`calc_mdd()` gives the minimum detectable difference of the same test
(Brock et al. 2015, eq. 2): the critical value times the standard error of
the difference, back-transformed to a percentage of the control (eq. 5 and
6) and classified (Table 1: class 0 above 100 %, class IV below 50 %).

```{r}
mdd <- calc_mdd(tw)
mdd[mdd$concentration == 200 & mdd$time == 56 & !is.na(mdd$mdd_pct),
    c("taxon", "control_value", "effect_pct", "mdd_pct", "mdd_class")]
```

This MDD has no power term: a true difference equal to it is detected about
half of the time. The estimated effect and its interval (`difference`,
`lower`, `upper`) are returned with it, because, as Mair et al. (2020)
argue, the interval is the better guide to how large an undetected effect
could be.

```{r, eval = has_plots, fig.height = 6}
plot_mdd(mdd, xlab = "Day")
```

## Community effects: principal response curves

`fit_prc()` fits the PRC of van den Brink and ter Braak (1999) with
`vegan::prc()`. The sign of the axis is arbitrary; by default it is set so
that the highest concentration goes down.

```{r}
prc <- fit_prc(d)
prc
```

`test_prc()` tests the first axis by permuting the complete time series of
the mesocosms, and each date with a redundancy analysis:

```{r}
test_prc(prc, n_perm = 499)
```

```{r, eval = has_plots, fig.height = 5}
plot_prc(prc, xlab = "Day")
```

Taxa with positive weights follow the curves (they decline where the curve
goes down); taxa with negative weights go the opposite way.

## Community NOECs

`community_noec()` applies Williams' test to the scores of the first axis of
a principal component analysis of each date, as Amador et al. (2024). The
direction of a principal component is arbitrary, so the table shows no
arrows.

```{r}
cn <- community_noec(d, pre_times = -7)
noec_table(cn)
cn$pca
```

Amador P, Vega C, Navarro Pacheco NI, Moratalla-López J, Palacios J,
Crettaz Minaglia MC, López I, Díaz M, Rico A (2024). Effects of the
fungicide azoxystrobin in two habitats representative of Mediterranean
coastal wetlands: a mesocosm experiment. *Aquatic Toxicology* 267, 106828.
<https://doi.org/10.1016/j.aquatox.2023.106828>

Brock TCM, Hammers-Wirtz M, Hommen U, Preuss TG, Ratte H-T, Roessink I,
Strauss T, Van den Brink PJ (2015). The minimum detectable difference (MDD)
and the interpretation of treatment-related effects of pesticides in
experimental ecosystems. *Environmental Science and Pollution Research* 22,
1160–1174. <https://doi.org/10.1007/s11356-014-3398-2>

Mair MM, Kattwinkel M, Jakoby O, Hartig F (2020). The minimum detectable
difference (MDD) concept for establishing trust in nonsignificant results:
a critical review. *Environmental Toxicology and Chemistry* 39, 2109–2123.
<https://doi.org/10.1002/etc.4847>

van den Brink PJ, ter Braak CJF (1999). Principal response curves: analysis
of time-dependent multivariate responses of biological community to stress.
*Environmental Toxicology and Chemistry* 18, 138–148.
<https://doi.org/10.1002/etc.5620180207>

Williams DA (1971). A test for differences between treatment means when
several dose levels are compared with a zero dose control. *Biometrics* 27,
103–117. <https://doi.org/10.2307/2528930>

Williams DA (1972). The comparison of several dose levels with a zero dose
control. *Biometrics* 28, 519–531. <https://doi.org/10.2307/2556164>
